SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vaginosis (SH f:
What & Why — the GUM-Clinic Angle

In a sexual health setting, BV matters for a slightly different reason than in gynaecology. It’s the single commonest cause of abnormal vaginal discharge presenting to GUM, and the clinician’s first job is to place it correctly on the STI-vs-not-STI map: BV is NOT a sexually transmitted infection, but it is sexually associated (more common with new/multiple partners + unprotected sex) and, crucially, it increases susceptibility to acquiring true STIs, including HIV.

So in GUM, BV is both a discharge to diagnose and treat and a flag that prompts full STI screening.
The mechanism (unchanged): loss of protective lactobacilli → vaginal pH rises above 4.5 → overgrowth of anaerobes (chiefly Gardnerella vaginalis). Everything flows from that loss of acidity. (See the Obs & Gynae “Pelvic & Vaginal Infections” note for the full clinical work-up.)
The Decisive Fork (SH version) — STI, or Not?

In GUM the discharge differential is framed explicitly by transmissibility — because it dictates partner notification:

BVTrichomoniasisCandidaChlamydia/Gonorrhoea
STI?No (sexually associated)YesNoYes
DischargeThin, white/grey, fishyFrothy, yellow-greenThick, white, curdyOften none; mucopurulent
pH>4.5>4.5<4.5—
ItchMinimalYesProminent—
Partner Rx?NoYesNoYes
The GUM teaching point: BV and trichomoniasis look similar (both raise pH, both can smell fishy), but only trichomoniasis triggers partner notification + contact tracing. Getting the STI/not-STI call right is the whole reason for accurate diagnosis here.
Sexual-Risk Associations (the SH emphasis)
  • More common with a new sexual partner, multiple partners, and unprotected sex — though it also occurs in women who’ve never been sexually active (hence “associated”, not “transmitted”)
  • Receptive oral sex, douching, and some hygiene practices disturb the flora
  • Increases the risk of acquiring STIs including HIV (raised pH + loss of the lactobacillus barrier), and increases onward HIV transmission risk
  • Associated with post-procedural infection (e.g. after TOP/IUD insertion) and, in pregnancy, adverse outcomes
Diagnosis — Amsel’s Criteria (≥3 of 4)
  • Thin, white, homogenous discharge
  • Vaginal pH >4.5
  • Clue cells on microscopy
  • Positive whiff/amine test (fishy odour with KOH)
In GUM this is often done at the point of care with narrow-range pH paper + microscopy of a wet/Gram-stained slide (Hay-Ison/Nugent grading is the lab equivalent).
Management — with the SH Additions (BASHH)
  • Asymptomatic BV usually needs no treatment (except pre-procedure or in pregnancy with risk factors)
  • First-line: oral metronidazole 400 mg BD for 5–7 days (or 2 g single dose / topical metronidazole gel / topical clindamycin). Avoid alcohol (disulfiram-like reaction)
  • Advice: avoid douching / vaginal soaps / shower gels — the key preventive measure
🔬 SH-specific — screen
  • Offer a full STI screen — BV is a marker of sexual-risk exposure + frequently co-exists with STIs
  • Test for chlamydia + gonorrhoea (NAAT), trichomonas, and offer HIV + syphilis serology
👥 SH-specific — partners
  • Do NOT treat male partners — partner treatment does not reduce recurrence (the key contrast with true-STI management)
  • Female partners: BV is more concordant in women who have sex with women — consider assessment, though routine partner treatment still isn’t recommended
Recurrence is common (~50–70% within a year) — address modifiable factors; suppressive regimens for frequent recurrence. Pregnancy: treat symptomatic BV (linked to preterm birth, miscarriage, PROM, chorioamnionitis, low birth weight, postpartum endometritis) — oral metronidazole; avoid the high-dose single regimen.
Exam Pearls (SH-oriented)
What it is
Commonest cause of abnormal discharge; NOT an STI but sexually ASSOCIATED (new/multiple partners, unprotected sex).
Why it matters in GUM
Increases risk of acquiring STIs including HIV.
Discharge
Thin white FISHY, pH >4.5, no itch — vs trichomonas (STI, frothy green) and candida (not STI, itchy, pH <4.5).
Amsel’s (≥3 of 4)
Thin discharge + pH >4.5 + clue cells + positive whiff. Point-of-care pH + microscopy in GUM.
1st-line
Oral metronidazole 400 mg BD 5–7 days. Avoid alcohol; avoid douching.
SH management
Full STI screen (chlamydia/gonorrhoea NAAT, trichomonas, HIV, syphilis) — but do NOT treat partners (unlike true STIs).
Recurrence / pregnancy
High recurrence; treat in pregnancy (preterm birth risk).
SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (genital):
What & Why

Vaginal candidiasis (“thrush”) is a symptomatic fungal infection of the vulva and vagina, usually caused by the yeast Candida. It’s extremely common (most women have at least one episode), it’s the itchy, non-STI member of the vaginal-discharge trio (the key contrast with BV and trichomonas), and recurrent disease has its own examinable management + prompts a search for an underlying cause (diabetes).

The organism & concept: ~80% Candida albicans. Candida can colonise the vagina asymptomatically and only cause infection when the local balance shifts — which is why the risk factors are all states that disturb flora or immunity.
The Decisive Fork — Candida vs BV vs Trichomonas

Thrush is the itchy, normal-pH, not-an-STI one — the pH is the cleanest discriminator:

Candida (thrush)Bacterial vaginosisTrichomoniasis
CauseYeast (not STI)Anaerobes (not STI)Protozoan (STI)
DischargeThick, white, “cottage cheese”Thin, white/greyFrothy, yellow-green
OdourNon-offensiveFishyOffensive
pH<4.5 (NORMAL)>4.5>4.5
ItchProminentMinimalYes
Partner Rx?NoNoYes
Risk Factors (anything disturbing flora/immunity)
  • Diabetes mellitus (especially poorly controlled)
  • Broad-spectrum antibiotics (wipe out protective bacteria)
  • Pregnancy (high oestrogen)
  • Immunosuppression (steroids, HIV, chemotherapy)
  • High oestrogen states; sometimes the COCP
Clinical Features
  • “Cottage cheese”, thick, non-offensive white discharge
  • Vulval itch and irritation (the dominant symptom)
  • Vulvitis: superficial dyspareunia, dysuria (external, from inflamed vulva)
  • Vulval erythema, fissuring, and satellite lesions on examination
Investigations
  • A high vaginal swab is NOT routinely needed if the picture is typical — diagnose clinically and treat
  • Vaginal pH — the key bedside test: candida pH <4.5 (normal) vs BV/trichomonas pH >4.5
  • HVS for microscopy/culture (MCS) — reserved for recurrent, atypical, or treatment-failure cases (identifies non-albicans species, e.g. C. glabrata)
  • Candida may be an incidental Pap smear finding (hyphae/spores) — but a smear is not the diagnostic test
Management (BASHH/NICE)
💊 Uncomplicated (non-pregnant)
  • 1st-line: single-dose oral fluconazole 150 mg
  • 2nd-line (oral contraindicated/not tolerated): clotrimazole 500 mg intravaginal pessary (single dose)
  • If vulval symptoms → add a topical imidazole cream (clotrimazole) to the vulva
  • Oral + topical azoles have similar cure rates — patient preference
🤰 Pregnancy
  • Do NOT use oral fluconazole (risk of congenital abnormalities)
  • Topical only — an intravaginal azole (clotrimazole) pessary/cream, often a longer course (up to 7 days)
Recurrent candidiasis (≥4 symptomatic episodes/year)
  • Check compliance with previous treatment
  • Confirm the diagnosis: HVS for MCS (species/resistance) + check blood glucose / HbA1c to exclude diabetes
  • Exclude differentials — e.g. lichen sclerosus, dermatitis, other causes of vulval itch
Induction–maintenance regimen: Induction — oral fluconazole every 3 days for 3 doses (days 1, 4, 7). Maintenance — oral fluconazole 150 mg weekly for 6 months. Advice: avoid vaginal irritants (soaps, douching); note some topical azoles damage latex condoms/diaphragms.
Exam Pearls
What it is
Symptomatic Candida (80% C. albicans); NOT an STI; the itchy, normal-pH member of the discharge trio.
Discharge
Thick, white, “cottage cheese”, non-offensive + vulval itch; pH <4.5 (NORMAL) — the key discriminator from BV/trichomonas.
Risk factors
Diabetes, antibiotics, pregnancy, immunosuppression, high oestrogen.
Diagnosis
Diagnose clinically → no routine swab (swab only if recurrent/atypical/treatment failure).
1st-line
Oral fluconazole 150 mg stat; 2nd-line clotrimazole 500 mg pessary; add topical azole for vulval symptoms.
Pregnancy
NO oral fluconazole → topical azole only.
Recurrent (≥4/yr)
Confirm (HVS + glucose/HbA1c), exclude lichen sclerosus, then induction (fluconazole every 3 days ×3) + maintenance (weekly ×6 months).
Partners
Not sexually transmitted → don’t treat partners.
SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia:
What & Why

Chlamydia is a sexually transmitted bacterial infection caused by Chlamydia trachomatis — the commonest STI in the UK. It’s mostly asymptomatic (so it spreads silently → the target of a national screening programme), and untreated infection causes serious reproductive complications — PID, ectopic pregnancy, and tubal infertility in women, epididymo-orchitis in men.

The organism: Chlamydia trachomatis — an obligate intracellular bacterium (it has a gram-negative-like envelope but is atypical and doesn’t Gram-stain well). Serovars D–K cause genital infection; L1–L3 cause LGV.
The National Chlamydia Screening Programme (NCSP)
  • Screen every sexually active person under 25 — annually, or on change of sexual partner
  • Everyone who tests positive is re-tested 3 months after treatment — this detects re-infection, NOT a test of cure (treatment is highly effective)
  • Standard GUM STI screen checks: Chlamydia, Gonorrhoea, Syphilis (blood), HIV (blood)
Clinical Features
Most cases are asymptomatic (~70% of women, ~50% of men) — the reason for screening.
WomenMenOn examination
Abnormal vaginal dischargeUrethral discharge/discomfortPelvic/abdominal tenderness
Pelvic painDysuriaCervical motion tenderness (excitation)
Abnormal bleeding (IMB/PCB)Epididymo-orchitisInflamed cervix, contact bleeding
Deep dyspareunia; dysuriaReactive arthritisPurulent/mucopurulent discharge
Investigations
  • Diagnosis by NAAT — highly sensitive/specific
  • First-line in women: vulvovaginal swab (self-taken is fine)
  • First-line in men: first-catch urine
  • Other sites by exposure: urethral, rectal swab (anal sex), pharyngeal swab (oral sex)
  • Test at all sites of potential exposure; offer a full STI screen
Management (BASHH)
First-line (uncomplicated): doxycycline 100 mg BD for 7 days (for urogenital, rectal + pharyngeal infection).
Currency point: the single 1 g azithromycin dose has been removed as a routine alternative — doxycycline is now clearly preferred (higher cure rates, especially for rectal infection and against co-existing Mycoplasma genitalium).
🤰 If doxycycline contraindicated (pregnancy, breastfeeding, tetracycline allergy)
  • Azithromycin 1 g stat, then 500 mg OD for 2 days (the 3-day regimen), OR
  • Erythromycin 500 mg QDS for 7 days
🔁 Test of cure (TOC)
  • Not routinely needed
  • Recommended in pregnancy, for rectal infection, and if symptoms persist
  • Do it ≥3–5 weeks after treatment (NAAT can stay positive from dead organisms)
General advice: no sex for 7 days and until all partners have completed treatment. Refer to GUM for contact tracing / partner notification (look back ~6 months / to the last partner). Test for other STIs.
Complications
♀️ Women
  • PID → chronic pelvic pain, tubal infertility, ectopic pregnancy
  • Fitz-Hugh-Curtis — perihepatitis (RUQ pain + adhesions)
  • Pregnancy/neonatal: ectopic, preterm birth, PROM, low birth weight, postpartum endometritis; neonatal conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum) + pneumonia (vertical transmission)
♂️ Men / both
  • Epididymo-orchitis
  • Reactive arthritis — “can’t see, can’t pee, can’t climb a tree” (conjunctivitis, urethritis, arthritis) — chlamydia is the classic trigger
  • Chlamydial conjunctivitis (autoinoculation)
Lymphogranuloma Venereum (LGV)

A chlamydial infection (serovars L1–L3) affecting lymphoid tissue; increasingly seen in MSM, often with HIV co-infection.

  • Primary: a small, transient painless genital/rectal ulcer or papule
  • Secondary: painful inguinal lymphadenopathy (“buboes”) / lymphadenitis
  • Tertiary: proctocolitis — change in bowel habit, anal pain, tenesmus, discharge (can mimic IBD in MSM)
Management: doxycycline 100 mg BD for 21 days (longer course than uncomplicated chlamydia); erythromycin/azithromycin are alternatives.
Exam Pearls
What it is
Chlamydia trachomatis = commonest UK STI; obligate intracellular; mostly ASYMPTOMATIC.
NCSP
Screen under-25s annually / on partner change; re-test positives at 3 months (for re-infection, not cure).
Diagnose
NAAT: vulvovaginal swab (women), first-catch urine (men); + rectal/pharyngeal by exposure.
1st-line
Doxycycline 100 mg BD × 7 days. (Single-dose azithromycin removed as routine option.)
Pregnancy/allergy
Azithromycin 1 g then 500 mg OD ×2 days, or erythromycin.
TOC
Not routine — but do in pregnancy, rectal infection, or persistent symptoms.
Advice
No sex 7 days + until partners treated; GUM referral for contact tracing.
Complications
PID → ectopic/infertility, epididymo-orchitis, reactive arthritis (can’t see/pee/climb), neonatal conjunctivitis & pneumonia, Fitz-Hugh-Curtis.
LGV
Serovars L1–L3, MSM: painless ulcer → buboes → proctocolitis; doxycycline 100 mg BD × 21 days.
SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orchitis:
What & Why

Epididymo-orchitis is inflammation of the epididymis (± the testis) — pain, swelling and inflammation triggered by infection. It’s a common cause of acute scrotal pain, and — critically — its key differential is testicular torsion, a surgical emergency that must be excluded urgently in younger men before you settle on this diagnosis.

The examinable essence: exclude torsion, work out the likely organism from age + sexual history, and treat accordingly — the causative organism (and antibiotic) splits cleanly by age.
The Decisive Fork — STI or Enteric Organism? (age & sexual history)
Younger men (<35), sexually activeOlder men (>35), low sexual risk
Likely causeSexually transmitted: C. trachomatis, N. gonorrhoeaeEnteric: E. coli (UTI/gram-negative organisms)
ContextNew/multiple partners, urethral dischargeRecent instrumentation/catheter, UTI, BPH/outflow problems
Investigation focusSTI screen (NAAT)MSU for MC&S
Causative agents (commonest→least): N. gonorrhoeae, C. trachomatis, E. coli, and (rarely) M. tuberculosis. Mumps orchitis is another non-STI cause.
Clinical Features
  • Scrotal pain and swelling — usually unilateral, developing over hours to days (more gradual than torsion)
  • Erythema of the overlying scrotum; testicular pain/tenderness
  • May have urethral discharge (STI cause), dysuria/urinary symptoms (enteric cause), fever
  • Prehn’s sign — pain relieved by elevating the testis (suggests epididymo-orchitis over torsion) — unreliable, never use it to exclude torsion
  • Cremasteric reflex usually present (contrast with torsion, where it’s typically absent)
The Critical Differential — Exclude Testicular Torsion
Testicular torsion is a surgical emergency and the key differential — especially in men <20. The testis must be salvaged within ~6 hours, so torsion is considered first in any acute scrotum.
🌀 Torsion clues
  • Sudden, severe pain (often <6 h), nausea/vomiting
  • High-riding testis with a horizontal lie
  • Absent cremasteric reflex; no urinary symptoms; younger patient
🔥 Epididymo-orchitis clues
  • More gradual onset
  • Urinary/urethral symptoms, fever
  • Cremasteric reflex present
If torsion cannot be excluded clinically → urgent surgical scrotal exploration, NOT imaging (don’t delay for an ultrasound).
Other differentials: inguinal hernia; testicular tumour (typically painless — a red flag if a mass persists).
Investigations
  • Exclude torsion first (clinical ± urgent exploration)
  • Young / STI likely: STI screen — first-catch urine + urethral swab NAAT for chlamydia + gonorrhoea; urethral Gram stain (gram-negative intracellular diplococci → gonorrhoea)
  • Older / low sexual risk: MSU for MC&S + urine dipstick (leucocytes/nitrites → enteric/UTI cause)
  • Scrotal ultrasound (Doppler) — assesses blood flow + supports the diagnosis, but must not delay exploration if torsion is suspected
Management (BASHH)

Treat empirically based on the likely cause (start before culture results):

① STI likely (young, sexually active)
  • Ceftriaxone 1 g IM single dose + doxycycline 100 mg PO BD for 10–14 days
  • Currency correction: use 1 g ceftriaxone (BASHH 2020, aligned with the gonorrhoea guideline for reduced-susceptibility strains) — not the older 500 mg
② Enteric/non-STI likely (older, low risk)
  • Ofloxacin 200 mg PO BD for 14 days (quinolone covering enteric organisms), or levofloxacin 500 mg OD
  • Note fluoroquinolone cautions (tendon/neuro/QT — MHRA)
③ Mixed STI + enteric risk (e.g. insertive anal sex): ceftriaxone 1 g IM + ofloxacin 200 mg BD for 14 days.
General: analgesia (NSAIDs), scrotal support/elevation, rest, fluids. If STI cause: no sex until treatment complete, refer to GUM for full screen + partner notification. Follow up; if not settling, re-image (?abscess, ?tumour).
Complications
  • Abscess formation, testicular infarction/atrophy, hydrocele/pyocele
  • Reduced fertility (especially bilateral)
  • Chronic epididymitis / chronic scrotal pain
Exam Pearls
What it is
Infective inflammation of the epididymis ± testis; common cause of acute scrotal pain.
Must-not-miss
ALWAYS exclude testicular torsion first (surgical emergency, salvage <6 h) — sudden severe pain, high-riding/horizontal testis, absent cremasteric reflex → urgent exploration, don’t wait for imaging.
Aetiology by age
<35 sexually active → chlamydia/gonorrhoea (STI); >35 low-risk → E. coli (enteric).
Investigate
Young → STI screen (urine/urethral NAAT); older → MSU MC&S.
STI treatment
Ceftriaxone 1 g IM + doxycycline 100 mg BD 14 days (update: 1 g, not 500 mg).
Enteric treatment
Ofloxacin 200 mg BD (or levofloxacin) 14 days.
STI cause
GUM referral + partner notification + no sex until treated.
Red flags
Painless mass = think tumour; mumps = a non-STI orchitis cause.
Complications
Abscess, infarction/atrophy, infertility, chronic pain.
SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea:
What & Why

Gonorrhoea is a sexually transmitted bacterial infection caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae — the second commonest bacterial STI (after chlamydia). It causes symptomatic infection more often than chlamydia (so it presents), untreated infection causes the same serious complications (PID, infertility, ectopic) plus disseminated infection, and — above all — it’s the poster child for antimicrobial resistance: gonococci have defeated penicillins, tetracyclines + quinolones, and ceftriaxone is now the last reliable first-line agent, with resistant strains already emerging.

The organism: a gram-negative diplococcus (“coffee-bean pairs”, seen intracellularly within neutrophils). It infects mucous membranes lined by COLUMNAR epithelium — endocervix, urethra, rectum, conjunctiva, pharynx — not squamous vaginal epithelium (a high-yield tropism point).
Clinical Features
Most patients ARE symptomatic (unlike chlamydia — a key contrast), though pharyngeal/rectal infections are often silent.
  • Odourless purulent discharge — often green or yellow (urethral in men; endocervical/vaginal in women)
  • Dysuria
  • Pelvic pain (women) / testicular pain or swelling (men — epididymo-orchitis)
  • Rectal infection — often asymptomatic; may cause anal discomfort/discharge
  • Prostatitis — perineal pain, urinary symptoms, tender prostate
  • Conjunctivitis — erythema, purulent discharge (adult autoinoculation, or neonatal)
Investigations
  • NAAT — the primary diagnostic test: endocervical / vulvovaginal / urethral swab (or first-catch urine); rectal + pharyngeal swabs in MSM / by exposure
  • ALSO take a charcoal swab for culture & sensitivities (MC&S) BEFORE treatment — essential because of high + rising resistance (NAAT confirms the organism but only culture gives sensitivities). This is what distinguishes gonorrhoea from chlamydia management
  • Urethral Gram stain — gram-negative intracellular diplococci gives a rapid presumptive diagnosis in symptomatic men
Management (BASHH)

The regimen depends on whether antibiotic sensitivities are known:

① Sensitivity UNKNOWN (empirical — usual)
  • Ceftriaxone 1 g IM single dose — MONOTHERAPY
  • Currency point: the older regimen added azithromycin 1 g — azithromycin is now DROPPED (rising resistance). Higher ceftriaxone dose covers reduced-susceptibility strains; dropping azithromycin reduces resistance pressure
② Sensitivity KNOWN (culture confirms)
  • Ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO single dose — used if the isolate is known ciprofloxacin-sensitive (avoids injection)
  • Only when susceptibility is confirmed (MHRA fluoroquinolone caution)
Test of cure (TOC) — recommended for ALL gonorrhoea cases (because of resistance; especially after pharyngeal infection or if symptoms persist). Timing: culture at ≥72 h; RNA NAAT at ≥7 days; DNA NAAT at ≥14 days after treatment (NAAT detects dead organisms if done too early).
General advice: no sex until treatment complete + TOC (7 days minimum). Refer to GUM; partner notification / contact tracing. Test for other STIs (chlamydia co-infection is common — but treat gonorrhoea specifically).
Key Complications
👶 Neonatal / emergency
  • Neonatal gonococcal conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum) — from the mother at birth; a medical emergency → can cause corneal perforation + blindness, associated with sepsis. Urgent treatment
🩸 Disseminated (DGI)
  • Haematogenous spread — the classic triad: dermatitis (pustular/haemorrhagic skin lesions), migratory polyarthritis/arthralgia, tenosynovitis
  • (± later purulent septic arthritis, rarely endocarditis/meningitis)
  • Local: PID → infertility, ectopic (women); epididymo-orchitis, prostatitis (men); urethral strictures
  • Increased HIV transmission
Exam Pearls
Organism / tropism
N. gonorrhoeae = gram-negative diplococcus; infects COLUMNAR epithelium (endocervix, urethra, rectum, conjunctiva, pharynx) — not squamous vagina.
vs chlamydia
More often SYMPTOMATIC; purulent green/yellow discharge + dysuria.
Diagnose
NAAT + ALWAYS a charcoal swab for culture & sensitivities (because of resistance).
1st-line
Ceftriaxone 1 g IM single dose — MONOTHERAPY (azithromycin now dropped).
If sensitive
Ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO only if the isolate is known sensitive.
TOC
Test of cure for ALL cases (culture ≥72 h / RNA NAAT ≥7 d / DNA NAAT ≥14 d).
Advice
GUM referral + partner notification + no sex until treated & TOC.
Complications
Neonatal conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum — emergency, blindness), DGI (dermatitis + migratory polyarthritis + tenosynovitis), PID/infertility.
AMR
Ceftriaxone is the last reliable first-line agent; resistant strains emerging.
SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical staging, AR:
What & Why

HIV is a retrovirus that infects and destroys CD4 T-helper cells, progressively crippling cell-mediated immunity until the patient becomes vulnerable to opportunistic infections and malignancies — the point at which it becomes AIDS. It’s a chronic, treatable, lifelong condition where modern antiretroviral therapy (ART) gives near-normal life expectancy and renders the person non-infectious (U=U); and where prevention (PrEP, PEP) and preventing vertical transmission are highly examinable.

The organism: HIV is an RNA retrovirus — HIV-1 (commonest worldwide) and HIV-2 (less common, West Africa). It enters + destroys CD4 T-helper cells; AIDS occurs when depletion leaves the patient immunocompromised.
Transmission
  • Unprotected anal, vaginal, or oral sex (anal receptive = highest risk)
  • Vertical transmission (in utero, at delivery, breastfeeding)
  • Infected blood/body fluids — needlestick, sharing needles, mucous-membrane/open-wound exposure
U=U (“Undetectable = Untransmittable”): a person on effective ART with a sustained undetectable viral load cannot transmit HIV sexually — a foundational modern principle.
Natural History & Clinical Stages
1
Primary HIV / seroconversion2–4 weeks post-infection: glandular-fever-like illness (fever, malaise, maculopapular rash, sore throat, lymphadenopathy, mouth ulcers). Often missed; very infectious
↓
2
Asymptomatic / clinical latencyoften years; virus replicating, CD4 slowly falling
↓
3
Symptomatic HIVconstitutional symptoms + minor opportunistic conditions (oral candidiasis, seborrhoeic dermatitis, shingles)
↓
4
AIDSCD4 low enough for AIDS-defining illnesses
AIDS-Defining Illnesses
  • Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) — dry cough, exertional desaturation (CD4 <200)
  • Kaposi’s sarcoma — caused by HHV-8; purple papules/plaques on skin/mucosa (GI/respiratory); radiotherapy/resection ± systemic therapy
  • Cytomegalovirus (CMV) — retinitis, colitis (CD4 <50)
  • Oesophageal/bronchial candidiasis
  • Lymphomas (including CNS lymphoma — EBV)
  • Tuberculosis (any CD4 — commonest globally)
  • Also: cerebral toxoplasmosis, cryptococcal meningitis, PML
Diagnosis & Monitoring
Diagnosis: 4th-generation lab test (HIV antibody + p24 antigen) — the standard; detects from ~4 weeks (confirm/repeat per window period). Point-of-care/self-tests available.
🔢 CD4 count (normal 500–1200 cells/mm³)
  • <200 = high risk of opportunistic infections / AIDS
🧬 HIV viral load (RNA copies/mL)
  • Marker of viral activity; thousands+ if untreated
  • Goal = undetectable (<50 copies/mL) on ART
Management — Antiretroviral Therapy (ART) (BHIVA)
ART is offered to EVERYONE with HIV, regardless of CD4 count (start as soon as possible after diagnosis).
  • Drug classes: NRTIs, NNRTIs, protease inhibitors, integrase inhibitors (INSTI), entry inhibitors
  • Standard first-line: 2 NRTIs + a third agent (now usually an integrase inhibitor) — e.g. tenofovir + emtricitabine + bictegravir (or dolutegravir)
  • Aim: sustained undetectable viral load → immune recovery + U=U
  • Long-acting injectable ART (cabotegravir + rilpivirine, 2-monthly) is now an option for those who prefer not to take daily pills
Additional care: CD4 <200 → prophylactic co-trimoxazole against PCP. Annual cervical smears (↑ HPV/cervical cancer risk). Vaccinations (avoid live vaccines if severely immunosuppressed), CVD risk management, bone/renal monitoring, mental health support.
Preventing Vertical Transmission
  • Mode of delivery by maternal viral load: <50 copies/mL → vaginal delivery; 50–400 → consider pre-labour CS; >400 → pre-labour caesarean
  • Unknown/>1000 copies/mL → IV zidovudine during labour
  • Neonatal PEP: low-risk (maternal load <50) → zidovudine monotherapy 2–4 weeks; high-risk → combination (zidovudine + lamivudine + nevirapine) for 4 weeks
  • Infant feeding: UK default is formula feeding; if the mother is fully suppressed on ART and chooses to breastfeed, this can be supported with close monitoring (BHIVA)
Prevention — PrEP & PEP
🛡️ PrEP (Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis)
  • ART taken by HIV-NEGATIVE people at ongoing risk to prevent acquisition
  • Tenofovir + emtricitabine (Truvada) — daily, or “event-based” (2-1-1) dosing for MSM
  • Offered to those at higher risk; requires regular HIV testing + renal monitoring. Highly effective when adherent
💊 PEP (Post-Exposure Prophylaxis)
  • ART started AFTER a potential exposure to prevent seroconversion
  • Commence ASAP + within 72 hours (the sooner the better; useless after 72 h)
  • Regimen: Truvada (emtricitabine/tenofovir) + raltegravir (or dolutegravir) for 28 days
  • HIV test at baseline + follow-up; covers sexual (PEPSE) + occupational (needlestick) exposure
Exam Pearls
What it is
RNA retrovirus destroying CD4 T-helper cells; HIV-1 (common) / HIV-2. AIDS = immunocompromise from CD4 depletion.
Seroconversion
Glandular-fever-like (fever, rash, sore throat, lymphadenopathy) 2–4 weeks post-infection.
Diagnose / monitor
4th-gen antibody/p24 antigen test. CD4 (<200 = AIDS risk) + viral load (goal undetectable).
U=U
Undetectable viral load = cannot transmit sexually.
ART
For everyone: 2 NRTIs + integrase inhibitor (e.g. tenofovir + emtricitabine + bictegravir).
Prophylaxis
CD4 <200 → co-trimoxazole PCP prophylaxis. Annual cervical smears.
AIDS illnesses
PCP, Kaposi’s (HHV-8), CMV, oesophageal candida, TB, lymphoma, toxoplasmosis, cryptococcus.
Vertical transmission
By viral load: <50 vaginal / >400 pre-labour CS; neonatal zidovudine PEP; UK default formula feed.
PrEP / PEP
PrEP (tenofovir/emtricitabine) = HIV-negative, prevent acquisition. PEP (Truvada + raltegravir, 28 days) = after exposure, within 72 h.
SEXUAL HEALTH__HPV / Genital Warts:
What & Why

Genital warts are benign epithelial growths caused by the human papillomavirus (HPV) — the second commonest STI diagnosed in UK sexual health services (after chlamydia). They’re very common, highly transmissible, benign but distressing, and open the door to the broader HPV story — the same virus family causes cervical, anal, vulval, penile + oropharyngeal cancers, which is why HPV vaccination and cervical screening are woven in.

The core distinction — low-risk vs high-risk HPV: HPV 6 & 11 cause warts; HPV 16 & 18 cause cancer — and the vaccine (Gardasil 9) covers both.
🟢 HPV 6 & 11 (“low-risk”)
  • Cause ~90% of genital warts
  • Do NOT cause cancer
🔴 HPV 16 & 18 (“high-risk”)
  • Cause ~70% of cervical cancer (+ other anogenital/oropharyngeal cancers)
  • Do NOT typically cause warts
Clinical Features
  • Painless lumps on the genitals or anal area
  • Either keratinised (hard) or non-keratinised (soft) — a distinction that guides treatment
  • Areas traumatised during intercourse commonly affected (introitus, penis, perianal skin)
  • May be single or multiple; occasionally itch, bleed, or cause distress; usually a clinical diagnosis (biopsy only if atypical/pigmented/suspicious)
Management (BASHH)

Choice guided by number/type/site + patient preference:

1️⃣ First-line
  • Topical podophyllotoxin — best for multiple, non-keratinised (soft) warts; patient-applied at home
  • Cryotherapy (liquid nitrogen) — best for solitary, keratinised (hard) warts; clinician-applied
2️⃣ Second-line / resistant
  • Topical imiquimod (immune-response modifier) — larger/keratinised warts or if 1st-line fails; lower recurrence than podophyllotoxin
  • Trichloroacetic acid, surgical excision/electrocautery/laser — difficult, extensive, or recurrent warts
BASHH: no single treatment is superior — choice by patient preference, wart morphology + site; patients can switch if response is limited.
Key principles
  • Recurrence is common (~30%) — warn the patient; warts can recur after apparent clearance
  • Contact tracing/partner notification is NOT required (unlike bacterial STIs) — partners can be assessed if they wish
🤰 Pregnancy + wider care
  • Podophyllotoxin + imiquimod are contraindicated → use cryotherapy (rarely, extensive warts → neonatal laryngeal papillomatosis)
  • Offer a full STI screen; discuss psychosexual wellbeing; encourage HPV vaccination + continued cervical screening
HPV Vaccination (the prevention story)
  • Gardasil 9 — the current UK vaccine — protects against HPV 6, 11 (warts) + 16, 18 (cancer) plus five more high-risk types
  • UK programme: offered to all children in school Year 8 (age 12–13), both boys and girls — now a single dose (since Sept 2023). Also offered to MSM up to 45 (2-dose schedule if ≥25) and other at-risk groups
  • Given before sexual debut for maximum benefit — has dramatically reduced both genital warts and pre-cancerous cervical lesions where uptake is high
Exam Pearls
What it is
Genital warts = HPV, usually types 6 & 11 (low-risk, ~90% of warts, benign).
High-risk HPV
16 & 18 → ~70% of cervical cancer (different types from warts).
Features
Painless keratinised (hard) or non-keratinised (soft) anogenital lumps.
1st-line
Podophyllotoxin (multiple soft warts) or cryotherapy (solitary hard warts). 2nd-line: imiquimod (lower recurrence).
Key points
Recurrence ~30% is common. Contact tracing NOT required (contrast with bacterial STIs).
Pregnancy
Avoid podophyllotoxin/imiquimod → cryotherapy.
Vaccine
Gardasil 9 (Year 8, both sexes, single dose) covers 6/11 + 16/18 → prevents warts AND cancer.
Also
Still attend cervical screening; offer full STI screen.
SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital):
What & Why

Genital herpes is a chronic, recurrent, sexually transmitted viral infection caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV). It’s extremely common, incurable (lifelong latency with recurrences), causes painful genital ulceration, and — most importantly for exams — carries a serious risk of neonatal herpes if a woman acquires it near delivery, which drives specific pregnancy management.

The mechanism: after initial infection, the virus becomes latent in the sensory nerve ganglia — the trigeminal ganglion for cold sores, the sacral ganglia for genital herpes — and reactivates to cause recurrent episodes.
HSV-1
  • Classically cold sores (oral), often acquired in childhood, dormant in the trigeminal ganglion
  • Genital HSV-1 acquired via oro-genital sex — now a common cause of first-episode genital herpes
HSV-2
  • Typically causes genital herpes; mostly an STI
  • Tends to recur more often than genital HSV-1
Clinical Features
  • May be asymptomatic, or symptoms appear months/years later on reactivation; when symptomatic, features usually appear within ~2 weeks of exposure
  • Painful genital ulceration or vesicular (blistering) lesions — the hallmark (vesicles → painful ulcers → crusting)
  • PRIMARY (first) infection is more severe than recurrences — systemic symptoms (headache, fever, malaise), extensive painful lesions, tender inguinal lymphadenopathy
  • Dysuria (from lesions); sometimes urinary retention (severe primary) or aseptic meningitis (rare)
  • Recurrent episodes — shorter, milder, often preceded by a prodrome (tingling/burning), and less frequent over time
Investigations
  • NAAT (HSV PCR) of a swab from the lesion base — the gold standard (also types HSV-1 vs HSV-2)
  • HSV serology (type-specific antibodies) — useful in recurrent ulceration of unknown cause, or to establish whether a pregnancy episode is primary vs recurrent
  • Tzanck smear / cytology: multinucleated giant cells — the “3 M’s”: Multinucleation, Margination of chromatin, Molding of nuclei (non-specific; PCR preferred)
Management (BASHH)
No cure — treatment shortens episodes + reduces severity/transmission. Advise saline bathing, analgesia, topical lidocaine, fluids, and abstain from sex during active lesions.
🔴 First (primary) episode
  • Oral aciclovir 400 mg three times daily for 5 days (start within 5 days of onset or while new lesions forming)
  • Valaciclovir 500 mg BD is an alternative. Cold sores → topical aciclovir
🔁 Recurrent episodes
  • Often mild + self-limiting → supportive care may suffice
  • Episodic antiviral (short courses) for troublesome recurrences
  • Suppressive therapy for frequent recurrences (≥6/year): aciclovir 400 mg BD (or valaciclovir 500 mg OD)
SH measures: GUM referral, full STI screen, discuss transmission (shedding occurs even when asymptomatic → condoms reduce but don’t eliminate risk), psychological support. Contact tracing is not routinely required (as with warts).
Herpes in Pregnancy & Neonatal HSV (BASHH/RCOG)
The danger: neonatal HSV is contracted mainly from active genital lesions/viral shedding during vaginal delivery → devastating disseminated/CNS disease. Risk is highest when the mother acquires a PRIMARY infection in the third trimester (no time to develop/transfer protective antibodies).
🤰 Primary infection in pregnancy
  • First episode >28 weeks (3rd trimester): elective caesarean recommended (transmission risk very high); oral aciclovir for the episode, then daily suppressive aciclovir 400 mg TDS until delivery
  • First episode <28 weeks: treat the episode; suppressive aciclovir 400 mg TDS from 36 weeks; vaginal delivery if no lesions at term
🔁 Recurrent genital herpes in pregnancy
  • Much lower neonatal risk (maternal antibodies protect the baby)
  • Suppressive aciclovir from 36 weeks; vaginal delivery appropriate even with a history of recurrences, provided no active lesions at labour
  • Active lesions at onset of labour → consider caesarean
Breastfeeding: aciclovir/valaciclovir are safe (minimal transfer). Avoid direct lesion contact with the baby; cold-sore precautions (no kissing the neonate).
Exam Pearls
Mechanism
HSV-1 or HSV-2; latent in SACRAL ganglia (genital) / trigeminal (oral), reactivates.
Strains
HSV-1 = usually oral/cold sores (genital via oro-genital sex); HSV-2 = usually genital, recurs more.
Features
Painful vesicles → ulcers; PRIMARY episode severe (fever, malaise, tender inguinal nodes); recurrences milder.
Diagnose
NAAT/PCR of lesion (gold standard); Tzanck “3 M’s” (multinucleation, margination, molding).
Treatment
1st episode: oral aciclovir 400 mg TDS × 5 days. Frequent recurrences (≥6/yr): suppressive aciclovir 400 mg BD.
Key points
No cure; shedding occurs when asymptomatic; contact tracing not required.
Pregnancy — primary
PRIMARY infection >28 weeks → elective caesarean + aciclovir + suppression to delivery.
Pregnancy — other
Primary <28 weeks or recurrent disease → suppressive aciclovir from 36 weeks, vaginal delivery if no lesions at term.
Neonatal
Neonatal HSV risk highest with maternal primary infection near term.
SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH framing):
What & Why — the GUM-Clinic Angle

In sexual health, PID matters as the most important preventable complication of untreated bacterial STIs — where an ascending chlamydia or gonorrhoea infection stops being a local, silent problem and starts causing tubal damage, infertility, and ectopic pregnancy. The GUM priority: very low threshold to treat empirically, identify + treat the causative STI, and notify + treat partners — PID is a sentinel event flagging an STI in the patient and their sexual network.

The core route: infection ascends from the endocervix → endometritis → salpingitis → oophoritis → pelvic peritonitis. The causative STIs are the same ones you screen for — which is why PID + STI screening are inseparable in GUM. (See the Obs & Gynae “Pelvic & Vaginal Infections” note for the full clinical work-up.)
The Decisive Fork (SH version) — Which STI Is Driving It?
OrganismGUM significance
Chlamydia trachomatisCommonest cause — often silent, so PID may be the first sign of infection
Neisseria gonorrhoeaeCauses more severe PID; drives the ceftriaxone-based regimen
Mycoplasma genitaliumIncreasingly recognised; may need specific (moxifloxacin) cover
Anaerobes / endogenous floraWhy metronidazole is included
GUM framing: ~a quarter of PID is caused by gonorrhoea or chlamydia identified on testing — but a negative STI test does NOT exclude PID (many cases are polymicrobial or test-negative), so you treat on clinical suspicion regardless.
Clinical Features
  • Lower abdominal pain (usually bilateral), deep dyspareunia, abnormal discharge, abnormal bleeding (IMB/PCB), fever, dysuria
  • On examination: cervical motion tenderness (“cervical excitation”) — the classic sign — plus adnexal/pelvic tenderness and cervicitis
Investigations — the STI-Screen-Driven Workup
  • Pregnancy test (β-hCG) — always, to exclude ectopic pregnancy
  • NAAT (endocervical/vulvovaginal swab) for chlamydia AND gonorrhoea — the central GUM test; also consider Mycoplasma genitalium
  • High vaginal swab for BV, candida, trichomonas
  • Microscopy — absence of pus cells makes PID unlikely (a useful rule-out); CRP/ESR often raised
  • Full STI screen including HIV + syphilis serology — because PID signals sexual-risk exposure
Key principle: PID is a clinical diagnosis — a negative swab doesn’t exclude it → start empirical treatment on suspicion rather than wait for results.
Management — with the GUM/Partner Dimension (BASHH)
Have a LOW threshold for empirical treatment — the diagnosis is uncertain and the complications of delay (infertility, ectopic, chronic pain) are serious.
✅ First-line
  • IM ceftriaxone 1 g single dose
  • + oral doxycycline 100 mg BD 14 days
  • + oral metronidazole 400 mg BD 14 days
Second-line
  • Oral ofloxacin 400 mg BD 14 days + metronidazole 400 mg BD 14 days
  • Per 2019 MHRA fluoroquinolone safety advice, quinolones are now second-line; avoid if gonococcal PID is likely (resistance)
The defining GUM step — partners: refer to GUM and notify/contact-trace — current + recent partners (look back ~6 months) should be assessed, tested, and treated empirically (usually chlamydia/gonorrhoea) to prevent “ping-pong” re-infection. No sex until the patient AND partner(s) have completed treatment.
In mild PID an intrauterine device can usually be left in situ. Test for other STIs (HIV, syphilis). Review at ~72 hours; if not improving, reconsider the diagnosis / consider admission (tubo-ovarian abscess).
Complications (the STI-Sequelae Emphasis)
  • Tubal factor infertility — risk rises with each PID episode (a key reason to treat STIs early)
  • Ectopic pregnancy (tubal scarring)
  • Chronic pelvic pain
  • Tubo-ovarian abscess (may need drainage/admission)
  • Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome — perihepatitis (RUQ pain + “violin-string” adhesions) from ascending chlamydial/gonococcal infection
Exam Pearls (SH-oriented)
What it is
Ascending endocervical infection; commonest STI cause = Chlamydia (gonorrhoea = more severe).
Classic sign
Cervical motion tenderness (excitation).
Always
β-hCG (exclude ectopic) + NAAT for chlamydia/gonorrhoea + full STI screen. Absence of pus cells makes PID unlikely.
Threshold
LOW threshold to treat empirically — don’t wait for swabs.
1st-line
IM ceftriaxone 1 g + doxycycline 14d + metronidazole 14d (quinolones now 2nd-line, MHRA).
Defining GUM step
GUM referral + partner notification/treatment + no sex until both treated.
Complications
Infertility, ectopic, chronic pelvic pain, tubo-ovarian abscess, Fitz-Hugh-Curtis.
SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies:
What & Why

Scabies is an intensely itchy skin infestation caused by the mite Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis, which burrows into the stratum corneum to lay eggs. It’s very common (UK care-home + household outbreaks), a key cause of generalised itch, can be sexually transmitted (hence its place in GUM as well as dermatology), and treatment failure is almost always a technique/contact problem rather than drug failure.

The core mechanism: the female mite burrows + lays eggs. The itch is a delayed type IV (T-cell) hypersensitivity reaction to the mite, its eggs + faeces — NOT the mite directly. This explains: (1) first infestation → symptoms at 4–6 weeks (time to sensitise); (2) re-infestation → itch within 1–3 days; (3) itch persists 2–6 weeks AFTER successful treatment (the immune reaction outlasts the dead mites) — not treatment failure.
Transmission
  • Prolonged skin-to-skin contact (the main route) — household, sexual partners, care settings
  • Sexual transmission — why it appears in GUM (genital lesions in adults)
  • Fomites (bedding/clothing) — a minor route in classic scabies (but major in crusted)
  • NOT related to poor hygiene — affects all social classes (a common misconception)
Clinical Features
  • Intense itch, characteristically WORSE AT NIGHT — the hallmark
  • Burrows — thin, greyish, wavy lines (mm–1 cm), the pathognomonic sign, best in finger web spaces, wrists (flexor), sides of fingers
  • Erythematous papules, excoriations, secondary eczematisation from scratching
  • Distribution: finger webs, wrists, elbows, axillae, waist/belt line, buttocks; in adults the genitals (penis/scrotum — often nodular; breasts/nipples in women)
  • In infants/elderly: can involve the palms, soles, face, scalp (spared in adults)
  • Household clustering — multiple itchy family members is a strong clue
Diagnosis
  • Largely CLINICAL — itch + burrows + typical distribution + affected contacts
  • Dermoscopy — the “delta-wing jet” sign (the mite at the end of a burrow)
  • Skin scraping microscopy — mites, eggs, or faecal pellets confirm it (low sensitivity; a negative doesn’t exclude)
The Decisive Fork — Classic vs Crusted (Norwegian) Scabies
Classic scabiesCrusted (Norwegian) scabies
Mite burdenA few (~10–15 mites)Thousands–millions
WhoAnyoneImmunocompromised, elderly, frail (HIV, steroids, learning disability)
AppearanceBurrows, papules, itchThick, hyperkeratotic, warty crusts; itch may be mild/absent
TransmissibilityModerateExtremely high (outbreaks)
TreatmentTopical permethrin ×2Topical scabicide + oral ivermectin (repeated) + isolation
Crusted scabies is a public-health emergency in institutions — it looks like psoriasis/eczema but is teeming with mites → isolate, treat aggressively, screen contacts.
Management (NICE CKS / BAD)
First-line: permethrin 5% cream. Success hinges on technique:
  • Apply to the WHOLE body from the neck down (adults) — including finger/toe webs, under the nails, genitals, buttocks, soles. In infants, elderly + immunocompromised, also treat the head, face, scalp (avoiding eyes)
  • Leave on 8–12 hours (e.g. overnight), then wash off; reapply to the hands if washed during the window
  • REPEAT the whole application after 7 days — the second dose kills newly hatched mites (eggs survive the first). Omitting the second dose is the commonest cause of “treatment failure”
💊 Second-line / alternatives
  • Malathion 0.5% aqueous lotion — if permethrin unsuitable (allergy)
  • Oral ivermectin (200 µg/kg, repeated ~day 8) — crusted scabies (with a topical agent), large outbreaks, or when topical is impractical. Not licensed <15 kg or in pregnancy
🚨 Critical universal steps
  • Treat ALL household members, sexual partners + close skin contacts at the SAME TIME — even if asymptomatic (pre-symptomatic window) — the key step to prevent “ping-pong” re-infestation
  • Decontaminate — wash clothing/bedding/towels at ≥50–60°C and/or seal in a bag for 72 h (mites die off-host in ~3 days)
Post-scabetic itch: emollients, a mild topical corticosteroid, + a non-sedating antihistamine — and reassure it doesn’t mean failure. Sexual contacts → consider GUM referral + full STI screen (scabies as an STI marker).
Complications
  • Secondary bacterial infection (impetiginisation — Staph/Strep) from scratching → and post-streptococcal complications (glomerulonephritis, rheumatic fever) in endemic settings
  • Crusted scabies → widespread outbreaks, secondary sepsis in the frail
  • Nodular scabies — persistent itchy nodules (genitals/groin) that can outlast treatment
Exam Pearls
What it is
Sarcoptes scabiei mite burrowing into skin; itch is a type IV hypersensitivity to the mite.
Presentation
Intense itch WORSE AT NIGHT + burrows in finger webs/wrists + household clustering + genital lesions.
Timing
First infestation → itch at 4–6 weeks; re-infestation → 1–3 days; itch persists 2–6 weeks AFTER cure (not failure).
1st-line
Permethrin 5% — whole body neck-down (+ head in infants/elderly), 8–12 h, REPEAT at 7 days.
Universal steps
Treat ALL close contacts simultaneously + decontaminate bedding/clothing (hot wash / bag 72 h).
Crusted (Norwegian)
Immunocompromised, thousands of mites, hyperkeratotic crusts, highly contagious → permethrin + oral ivermectin + isolate.
Post-scabetic itch
Emollient + mild steroid + antihistamine.
Complications / notes
Secondary bacterial infection (± post-strep GN), nodular scabies. NOT about hygiene; can be sexually transmitted → consider STI screen.
SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (NGU):
What & Why

Urethritis is inflammation of the urethra — the commonest STI presentation in men, typically causing dysuria and/or urethral discharge. It’s a syndrome, not a single organism — the first job is to split it into gonococcal (treat as gonorrhoea) vs non-gonococcal (NGU), then recognise that the leading NGU pathogens (chlamydia and Mycoplasma genitalium) drive both treatment and the growing problem of macrolide resistance.

Framing: presents with dysuria and/or urethral discharge — or asymptomatic. Divided into gonococcal urethritis and non-specific/non-gonococcal urethritis (NSU/NGU) — the first fork.
The Decisive Fork — Gonococcal or Non-Gonococcal?
Gonococcal urethritisNon-gonococcal (NGU/NSU)
OrganismNeisseria gonorrhoeaeChlamydia, M. genitalium, Ureaplasma, others
DischargeOften profuse, purulent, green/yellowOften scant, mucoid/clear
MicroscopyGram-negative intracellular diplococci presentPus cells (≥5 PMNs/hpf) but no diplococci
ManagementTreat as gonorrhoea (ceftriaxone 1 g)Doxycycline (see below)
Causes of NGU
  • Chlamydia trachomatis — the commonest identifiable cause (~a third of NGU)
  • Mycoplasma genitalium — the second commonest; increasingly important because of macrolide resistance
  • Ureaplasma urealyticum
  • Others: Trichomonas vaginalis, adenovirus, HSV, and non-infective/mechanical causes (trauma, catheter). A significant proportion are idiopathic
Clinical Features
  • Dysuria and/or urethral discharge (the key symptoms) — but many cases are asymptomatic
  • Urethral discomfort/itch, meatal irritation
  • Mycoplasma genitalium is not just urethritis — it also causes epididymitis, cervicitis, endometritis, PID, reactive arthritis, preterm delivery, tubal infertility (a chlamydia-like complication profile)
Investigations
  • NAAT — for chlamydia, gonorrhoea, and M. genitalium: first-catch (first-void) urine in men; vulvovaginal swab in women
  • Urethral smear microscopy — confirms urethritis (≥5 polymorphs/high-power field) + looks for gram-negative intracellular diplococci (→ gonorrhoea)
  • Full STI screen (HIV, syphilis)
For every M. genitalium-positive sample: test for MACROLIDE RESISTANCE, and perform a TEST OF CURE after treatment — because resistance is common and rising.
Management (BASHH)
🟢 Uncomplicated, first-presentation NGU
  • First-line: doxycycline 100 mg BD for 7 days (preferred over azithromycin — more effective vs M. genitalium and, crucially, does NOT induce macrolide resistance)
  • Alternatives: azithromycin 1 g stat then 500 mg OD ×2 days (extended — single-dose drives resistance, so avoided); ofloxacin 200 mg BD (or 400 mg OD) 7 days
🔁 Recurrent / persistent NGU
  • If first-line was doxycycline → azithromycin (1 g stat then 500 mg OD ×2) + metronidazole 400 mg BD 5 days
  • If first-line was azithromycin → moxifloxacin 400 mg OD 10 days + metronidazole 5 days, OR doxycycline + metronidazole
  • (Metronidazole covers Trichomonas/anaerobes; moxifloxacin covers macrolide-resistant M. genitalium)
Confirmed M. genitalium: macrolide-sensitive → doxycycline 7 days then extended azithromycin; macrolide-resistant → moxifloxacin. Always test of cure.
General advice: no sex until treatment complete (+ 7 days after, and until partners treated). GUM referral, partner notification/contact tracing, full STI screen.
Exam Pearls
What it is
Dysuria ± urethral discharge (often asymptomatic); split into gonococcal vs non-gonococcal (NGU/NSU).
NGU causes
Chlamydia (commonest), M. genitalium (2nd, resistance issue), Ureaplasma; also trich/HSV/adenovirus.
M. genitalium spectrum
Also causes epididymitis, cervicitis, endometritis, PID, reactive arthritis, tubal infertility, preterm birth.
Diagnose
NAAT (first-void urine men / vulvovaginal swab women) + urethral smear (≥5 PMNs/hpf; diplococci → gonorrhoea).
M. genitalium testing
Test every positive for MACROLIDE RESISTANCE + do a TEST OF CURE.
1st-line NGU
Doxycycline 100 mg BD 7 days (better vs M. genitalium, doesn’t drive resistance).
Recurrent
Add metronidazole; use moxifloxacin for macrolide-resistant M. genitalium.
Advice
GUM referral + partner notification + no sex until treated.
SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis:
What & Why

Syphilis is an STI caused by the spirochaete Treponema pallidum. It’s “the great imitator” — progressing through distinct stages over years, each with different (often deceptive) features; untreated it causes devastating late complications (neurosyphilis, cardiovascular syphilis) and congenital syphilis. Rates have risen sharply in the UK.

The organism: a spirochaete (spiral-shaped bacterium), mainly an STI. Incubation ~21 days (range 9–90) to the primary lesion. Transmission: oral/vaginal/anal sex (contact with an infectious lesion), vertical (→ congenital syphilis), IVDU, blood transfusion (rare).
The Decisive Fork — Which Stage?
1️⃣ Primary
  • Chancre — a PAINLESS, indurated genital ulcer at inoculation (highly infectious)
  • Local painless lymphadenopathy; heals spontaneously → often missed
2️⃣ Secondary (~6–10 wks)
  • A systemic, disseminated stage
  • Maculopapular rash on TRUNK, PALMS + SOLES
  • Condylomata lata (moist grey wart-like plaques), snail-track mouth ulcers, fever, lymphadenopathy, patchy alopecia
3️⃣ Latent
  • Asymptomatic — infection persists (positive serology, no signs)
  • Early latent (<2 years — potentially infectious) vs late latent (>2 years — non-infectious sexually, but can transmit vertically)
4️⃣ Tertiary (years later, ~⅓ untreated)
  • Gummas — granulomatous destructive lesions (skin, bone, organs)
  • Cardiovascular — aortitis → thoracic aortic aneurysm (ascending aorta), aortic regurgitation
  • Neurosyphilis (see below)
Exam contrast: syphilitic chancre = PAINLESS; chancroid (H. ducreyi) + herpes = painful. A painless genital ulcer → think syphilis.
Neurosyphilis & Congenital Syphilis
🧠 Neurosyphilis (can occur at ANY stage)
  • Headache, altered behaviour, dementia (general paresis)
  • Tabes dorsalis — dorsal column degeneration → sensory ataxia, lightning pains, loss of proprioception
  • Ocular syphilis, cranial nerve palsies
  • Argyll-Robertson pupil — small, irregular pupil that ACCOMMODATES but does NOT REACT to light
👶 Congenital syphilis
  • Hutchinson’s teeth (notched, peg-shaped incisors)
  • Rhagades, interstitial keratitis, sabre shins, saddle nose, sensorineural deafness
  • Hutchinson’s triad = teeth + keratitis + deafness
Investigations
Direct detection (from a lesion): dark-field microscopy + PCR of a swab from a chancre/lesion — detects T. pallidum directly (it can’t be routinely cultured).
Serology — a two-tier system
🧪 Treponemal (specific — confirm exposure)
  • EIA/CLIA (usual screen), TPHA/TPPA
  • Stay positive for life even after cure → confirm infection but can’t distinguish active from treated
📉 Non-treponemal (RPR / VDRL)
  • Sensitive but non-specific; quantitative (titres)
  • Reflect disease activity: titre falls with successful treatment, rises with active/reinfection → used to monitor response
  • Can give false positives (pregnancy, SLE/antiphospholipid, other infections) → always confirmed with a treponemal test
Neurosyphilis: lumbar puncture (CSF for VDRL, protein, cells).
Management (BASHH 2024)
Penicillin is first-line at EVERY stage — the drug of choice (now given with lidocaine for tolerability).
  • Early syphilis (primary, secondary, early latent): benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM as a single dose
  • Late latent / tertiary (non-neuro): benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU IM weekly for 3 doses (longer — the organism divides slowly)
  • Neurosyphilis: IV/procaine penicillin for ~14 days (± probenecid); add steroid cover
  • Penicillin allergy / alternative: doxycycline 100 mg PO BD for 14 days (28 days if late); ceftriaxone is an alternative. Macrolides no longer recommended (resistance). In pregnancy, penicillin is essential → desensitise if allergic (doxycycline contraindicated)
Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction: an acute febrile reaction within hours of the first antibiotic dose — fever, rash, tachycardia, headache, myalgia — from cytokine release as spirochaetes are killed en masse. Self-limiting → antipyretics (it is NOT an allergy). Can be dangerous in pregnancy (may trigger contractions/fetal distress) or neuro/cardiovascular syphilis (steroid cover).
General: GUM referral, partner notification/contact tracing, full STI screen (including HIV — co-infection common), no sex until treated + follow-up serology confirms response.
Exam Pearls
What it is
Treponema pallidum (spirochaete); “the great imitator”; incubation ~21 days.
Primary
PAINLESS chancre + painless local nodes (vs painful herpes/chancroid).
Secondary (6–10 wks)
Rash on TRUNK + PALMS + SOLES, condylomata lata, snail-track mouth ulcers, systemic symptoms.
Latent / tertiary
Latent = asymptomatic, positive serology (early <2 yrs / late >2 yrs). Tertiary = gummas, cardiovascular (aortic aneurysm/aortitis), neurosyphilis.
Neurosyphilis
Tabes dorsalis, general paresis/dementia, ARGYLL-ROBERTSON PUPIL (accommodates but doesn’t react).
Congenital
Hutchinson’s teeth, rhagades, keratitis, sabre shins, saddle nose, deafness.
Diagnosis
Dark-field microscopy/PCR of lesion; serology = treponemal (EIA/TPPA, positive for life) + non-treponemal (RPR/VDRL, titres track activity/treatment).
Treatment
PENICILLIN at every stage (benzathine single dose early; 3 weekly doses late; IV for neuro). Doxycycline if allergic (not in pregnancy).
Jarisch-Herxheimer
Fever/rash/tachycardia hours after first dose → antipyretics.
